input.dimension: Negative/zero interval behavior of the schedule library in test12_executable: confirming the `while next_run <= now: next_run += period` linear step loop (schedule/__init__.py line 734) and measuring its scaling
rules: Any negative value for --a, --b, or --c causes the corresponding `schedule.every(N).<unit>.do(...)` call to raise OverflowError inside `Job.do()` -> `Job._schedule_next_run()`. Process exits with code 1 (NOT 2, NOT 0).

The stderr on a negative interval is exactly these 7 lines, each terminated by 
 (no leading/trailing spaces, no blank lines):
"Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line 15, in <module>
    File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
    File "schedule/__init__.py", line 734, in _schedule_next_run
OverflowError: date value out of range
[PYI-523:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
" -- with the exact indentation being two spaces before each `File "..."` line. Verbatim byte-for-byte for --c: "Traceback (most recent call last):
", "  File "test12.py", line 15, in <module>
", "  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 657, in do
", "  File "schedule/__init__.py", line 734, in _schedule_next_run
", "OverflowError: date value out of range
", "[PYI-523:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
".

The traceback's `File "test12.py", line NN` frame identifies WHICH argument was negative, because the three schedule.every() calls are on distinct source lines: line 11 = --a (seconds), line 13 = --b (minutes), line 15 = --c (hours). An implementation must therefore emit line 11 for a negative --a, line 13 for a negative --b, line 15 for a negative --c. The inner two frames are always `schedule/__init__.py`, line 657, in do` and `schedule/__init__.py`, line 734, in _schedule_next_run`.
Only the two frames of schedule appear; there is no `raise` source line text shown for any frame (PyInstaller strips source, so no code echo lines under any `File ...` line).

stdout on a negative interval contains only the print() output that happened BEFORE the failing call, and it IS flushed even though the process dies from an unhandled exception (CPython flushes std streams at interpreter shutdown). For --a 5 --b 10 --c -N stdout is exactly "5
10
". For a negative --b it is exactly "<a>
". For a negative --a stdout is empty.

The failure is a walk-backwards loop, not an immediate check: schedule sets next_run = now + period (period negative => in the past), then steps `next_run += period` until the date underflows datetime.MINYEAR (year 1), which raises OverflowError: date value out of range. The number of loop iterations is therefore (now - datetime.min) / |period| ~= 17.76e6 / |hours| iterations as of 2026.

Wall time for a negative interval is startup + K/|interval_in_hours| where startup ~= 0.145 s and K ~= 0.93 s on this machine (i.e. ~52.6 ns per loop iteration, ~17.76 million iterations for a 1-hour step). The linear-step hypothesis HOLDS: |interval| * loop_time is constant to within ~4% over |interval| = 1..48 hours (0.935, 0.930, 0.942, 0.924, 0.920, 0.924, 0.936, 0.960).

Unit conversion is exact, so cost depends only on the absolute period length, not the unit: --a -3600 (seconds) must behave/scale identically to --c -1 (hours), and --a -86400 identically to --c -24, and --b -60 identically to --c -1. (Predicted from the fitted model; see gotchas -- I did not get to run these before being cut off.)

Passing 0 to --a, --b or --c makes the same line-734 loop spin forever (next_run += timedelta(0) never advances past now), so the process never terminates and must be killed. Under `timeout 10` expect rc=124. Because stdout is block-buffered when redirected to a pipe/file and the process is SIGTERM-killed, the pre-hang prints are LOST: expect completely empty stdout and empty stderr on a pipe. On a tty stdout is line-buffered, so the pre-hang lines (e.g. "5\n5\n" for --a 5 --b 5 --c 0) do appear. (Predicted; not executed -- see gotchas.)
Because a 0 interval hangs and small negative intervals can take minutes, never invoke the program under test without a wall-clock timeout.

Every statement about those is a prediction extrapolated from the fitted model T = 0.145 + 0.93/|hours| and from the known CPython buffering rules, not an observation. `script -qc` IS available at /usr/bin/script on this box, so the tty test is feasible -- it just wasn't run.

The linear-step hypothesis is CONFIRMED for negative intervals. Fit: loop_time_seconds = 0.93 / |interval_in_hours|, i.e. |interval| x loop_time is constant (0.920-0.960 across |iv| = 1,2,3,4,8,12,24,48). Table of |interval| (hours) vs total wall s vs loop-only s (= wall - 0.145 startup): 1 -> 1.080 / 0.935; 2 -> 0.610 / 0.465; 3 -> 0.459 / 0.314; 4 -> 0.376 / 0.231; 8 -> 0.260 / 0.115; 12 -> 0.222 / 0.077; 24 -> 0.184 / 0.039; 48 -> 0.165 / 0.020; 168 -> 0.157 / 0.012; 720 -> 0.146 / ~0.001; 8766 -> 0.142 / ~0.

You MUST subtract the ~0.145 s PyInstaller startup constant before testing proportionality. Raw wall times look sublinear (1.08 vs 0.14, only 7.6x across a 8766x interval range) purely because startup dominates for |iv| >= 100. Only the residual scales as 1/|interval|.

Per-iteration cost is only ~52.6 ns, which is far too fast for a `datetime.datetime.now()` call inside the loop body. This implies the comparison bound is hoisted/cached (a single `now` captured before the loop) and the body is just a timedelta add + compare. Do not model the loop as re-reading the clock each pass.

Beyond |interval| ~ 500 hours the loop cost is below measurement noise -- large negative intervals are indistinguishable from the success path in timing, so timing cannot be used to detect them; only the exit code / stderr can.

Wall times are machine-specific (measured on a 64-core Linux box, Python from a PyInstaller onefile bundle). Reproduce the 0.93 s constant locally rather than hard-coding it; what is portable is the 1/|interval| proportionality and the ~17.76e6/|hours| iteration count.

The iteration count depends on the CURRENT DATE (it is (now - datetime.min)/|period|), so the constant drifts upward by ~1/2026 per year. A test asserting absolute seconds will slowly rot; assert the ratio instead.

--a and --b negative values are much more expensive than --c because the unit is smaller: predicted --b -1 ~ 56 s of loop (60x the --c -1 case) and --a -1 ~ 3370 s (~56 min, 3600x). `timeout 8` will report rc=124 for both of these and they must NOT be mistaken for the 0-interval infinite hang -- they do eventually raise OverflowError. Distinguish them by giving --b -1 a ~90 s timeout; --a -1 realistically cannot be run to completion.

rc=124 is timeout's kill signal, not a program exit code; report it as a timeout, and note that a SIGTERM kill discards any block-buffered stdout, so a timed-out run on a pipe yields empty stdout even though the program had already printed.
